events.description: Tectonic corneoscleral lamellar anterior transplant with donor cornea and sclera

evidence.quote: A partial transplant was performed using a donor cornea, which was placed upside down in the artificial chamber with the endothelium facing upwards (Figure 2).
This was achieved using a micrometer diamond knife entering at a depth of 100 µm as peripherally as possible.
The sclera was then detached from the cornea through the limbus using scissors, leaving a sclera pedicle with a base of 4 mm and a width of 2 mm.
The receiving cornea was prepared by manually removing the epithelium with a type-15 scalpel.

The donor cornea was positioned over the recipient’s cornea and sutured through the limbus with superficial corneal sutures to the donor cornea and deep in the recipient’s limbus to allow perfect positioning and epithelial migration.
The donor sclera was similarly sutured over the thinned recipient sclera and covered with the patient’s inferior conjunctival epithelium.

summary.text: A 69-year-old man with T-cell cutaneous lymphoma and ocular rosacea was referred to ophthalmology for lesions in the ocular periphery of the right eye; best-corrected visual acuity was counting fingers at 3 m in the right eye and 1 m in the left eye. Toluidine blue staining showed three perilimbal conjunctival lesions, and neoadjuvant IFN-α2b every 6 h for four months was begun.

Ocular surface squamous neoplasia was suspected. After one month, topical 0.1% fluorometholone acetate and 0.02% MMC every 6 h for 14 days were prescribed for OCT findings suggestive of cancer cell invasion beyond the epithelium; MMC was suspended for 7 days and another 7-day cycle followed. The lesions regressed over two months, leaving a small stained area, and the scheduled excision was not performed.

At follow-up, conjunctival hyperemia and a total epithelial defect were observed; an MMC lesion was suspected and MMC was discontinued. Impression cytology showed a strong inflammatory reaction on the ocular surface attributed to recent topical MMC and was negative for dysplastic or neoplastic cells. A persistent epithelial defect and scleral show led to referral to the Oculoplastic Department, where no surgery was required.

Five months later he returned with moderate corneal edema, a 2.7 mm hypopyon, a corneal ulcer covering nearly all of the cornea, corneal melting and inferior corneoscleral thinning. Gentamicin, vancomycin and atropine produced no improvement, and he did not adhere to prescribed medroxyprogesterone. Although the infection improved, extreme thinning of the cornea and inferior sclera required a tectonic corneoscleral lamellar anterior transplant, performed as a partial transplant using a donor cornea and sclera.

In the first month after surgery he had no symptomatic complaints; the transplant adhered well with mild edema, BVCA was below 0.1, bidigital tonometry was normal and central pachymetry was 670 µm. At the four-month follow-up he still had no complaints, but corneal edema had worsened with epithelial microcysts and reactive miosis, scleral thinning was maintained, and he declined an indicated triple procedure for ocular rehabilitation.
